questions.question: How does @InjectMocks injection work under the hood?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Injection Strategy | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @InjectMocks tries three injection strategies in order: constructor injection (matching by type), setter injection, then field injection. If none succeed, it creates the object with no injection — no error is thrown, leading to null fields that cause NPE at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the internal resolution order of @InjectMocks and its silent failure mode
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming @InjectMocks will throw a clear error if injection fails — it does not, it silently continues with null fields
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three-phase injection order and connect this to why constructor injection in production code prevents these silent failures

sections.title: How @InjectMocks Resolves Dependencies
sections.content: **@InjectMocks** is a Mockito annotation that automates dependency injection for the class under test. When you annotate a field with @InjectMocks, Mockito tries to inject mocks (created with @Mock) into that object. WHY this matters: it reduces boilerplate in test setup. HOW it works: Mockito follows a three-phase strategy. First, it looks for a **constructor** that matches the available mocks by type, preferring the largest constructor. If that fails, it tries **setter methods** (setX methods matching mock types). If that also fails, it falls back to **field injection** via reflection. The danger: if none of these strategies succeed, Mockito **silently creates the object** with no dependencies injected. Fields remain null, causing **NullPointerException** when your test runs. Think of it like a delivery service with three fallback routes: front door (constructor), side door (setter), window (field). If all are locked, the package is just dropped on the lawn (null fields).

sections.title: Constructor Injection with @InjectMocks
Key Points
content: **Constructor injection**: Mockito's first choice, matches the largest constructor by mock types available
**Setter injection**: Second fallback, looks for setX methods matching mock types (rarely used in modern Spring)
**Field injection**: Final fallback, uses reflection to directly set private fields
**Silent failure**: If all three strategies fail, Mockito creates the object with null dependencies — no error thrown
**NullPointerException risk**: Tests fail at runtime when null dependencies are used, not at setup time
**MockitoExtension**: Using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) enables strict stubbing mode, which helps surface unused mocks
**Best practice**: Use constructor injection in production code so @InjectMocks can resolve dependencies predictably

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-InjectMocks works by trying three injection strategies in order. First, it looks for a constructor that matches your at-Mock fields by type. If your OrderService has a constructor taking OrderRepository and PaymentService, and you've got those as at-Mock fields, Mockito will call that constructor with the mocks. If there's no matching constructor, it tries setter injection — looking for methods like setOrderRepository. If that also fails, it falls back to field injection using reflection to directly set private fields. Here's the dangerous part: if none of these strategies work, Mockito doesn't throw an error. It just creates the object with null fields. Your test will compile fine, but you'll get a NullPointerException when the test actually runs and tries to use those dependencies. That's why constructor injection is the gold standard — it makes dependencies explicit and forces at-InjectMocks to use the most predictable path. If you're seeing NPEs in tests with at-InjectMocks, it's usually because Mockito couldn't match your mocks to any injection point. The fix is either add a constructor that matches your mocks, or skip at-InjectMocks entirely and manually construct the object in at-BeforeEach. That way, if the wiring is wrong, you'll get a compile-time error instead of a runtime surprise.

questions.question: Should you use field injection or constructor injection in production Spring services?
questions.title: Field vs Constructor Injection Spring | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Prefer constructor injection over @Autowired field injection. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, enables immutable final fields, works cleanly with @InjectMocks in tests, and fails fast if a dependency is missing — at startup rather than at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Spring best practices and can articulate the testability and immutability advantages of constructor injection
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defending field injection because it requires less code — missing the testability, immutability, and compile-time safety benefits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect constructor injection to test simplicity: at-InjectMocks works cleanly, and manual test setup is trivial with explicit constructors

sections.title: Constructor Injection vs Field Injection in Production
sections.content: **Constructor injection** is the recommended approach for Spring production services. WHY: it enforces immutability (fields can be final), makes dependencies explicit in the class signature, enables testing without reflection, and fails fast at startup if a dependency is missing. **Field injection** (using @Autowired on fields) is convenient but has hidden costs: fields can't be final, dependencies are invisible to callers, and tests require either Spring context or reflection hacks like ReflectionTestUtils. HOW constructor injection works: Spring sees a constructor with parameters and automatically resolves beans to pass as arguments. If a bean is missing, the app **fails to start** with a clear error. With field injection, the object is created first, then Spring tries to inject fields — if a field can't be injected, you might not discover it until that code path executes. Think of constructor injection as a contract: the class says upfront what it needs. Field injection is like a secret dependency list hidden inside the implementation.

sections.title: Constructor Injection (Recommended)
Key Points
content: **Immutability**: Constructor injection allows final fields, preventing accidental reassignment in the service's lifetime
**Explicit dependencies**: The constructor signature documents what the class needs — no hidden @Autowired fields to discover
**Fail-fast behavior**: If a dependency is missing, the application fails to start with a clear error, not at runtime
**Testability**: Pass mocks to the constructor in tests — no Spring context, no ReflectionTestUtils, no at-InjectMocks risk
**No @Autowired needed**: Modern Spring (4.3+) auto-detects a single constructor and injects without annotation
**Field injection drawback**: Can't make fields final, dependencies are hidden, testing requires reflection or full context
**Circular dependency detection**: Constructor injection surfaces circular dependencies immediately, field injection hides them until runtime

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You should absolutely prefer constructor injection in production Spring services. Here's why. First, it lets you make your dependencies final, which means once the service is constructed, those references can't be changed. That's huge for thread safety and reasoning about your code. Second, the constructor signature is a contract — anyone looking at the class can see exactly what it depends on. With field injection, you have to scan through the class to find all the at-Autowired annotations. Third, testing becomes trivial. You just pass mocks to the constructor in your test. No need for at-InjectMocks, no Spring context, no ReflectionTestUtils. If you mess up the wiring, you get a compile error, not a runtime surprise. Fourth, constructor injection fails fast. If Spring can't find a bean to inject, your app won't start — you'll see the error immediately in the logs. With field injection, the object gets created, and the missing dependency might not surface until that specific code path runs in production. The only argument for field injection is that it's less verbose, but that's a weak trade-off. Modern Spring doesn't even require at-Autowired on constructors anymore — if there's one constructor, Spring auto-wires it. So you're not saving much typing. The bottom line: constructor injection gives you compile-time safety, immutability, and simple tests. That's why it's the Spring team's official recommendation.

questions.question: How do you manually inject mocks without using @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Manual Mock Injection Without @InjectMocks | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Create the class under test manually in @BeforeEach, passing mocks as constructor arguments. This is explicit, debuggable, and fails loudly if arguments don't match. Preferred for complex setups where @InjectMocks silent failure would be hard to debug.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness that at-InjectMocks is optional and that manual construction can be clearer for complex scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using at-InjectMocks without recognizing when explicit construction is simpler and safer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Argue for explicit control when the test has conditional logic or multiple configurations of the same class

sections.title: Manual Mock Injection Without @InjectMocks
sections.content: **Manual injection** means constructing the class under test yourself in the test setup, passing mocks as constructor arguments. WHY do this: it's explicit, debuggable, and fails at compile time if you get the argument order wrong. There's no silent failure like @InjectMocks can have. HOW it works: create mocks with @Mock or Mockito.mock(), then in @BeforeEach, call new YourService(mockA, mockB). When should you prefer this over @InjectMocks? When you have **multiple configurations** of the same service (testing different constructor signatures), when you want **conditional logic** in setup (injecting different mocks based on test parameters), or when the class has a **complex dependency graph** where @InjectMocks might silently fail. Think of @InjectMocks as autopilot — great for standard cases, but manual control is safer when the landing is tricky. Manual injection is like driving stick shift: more control, but you're responsible for every gear change.

sections.title: Manual Mock Injection in @BeforeEach
Key Points
content: **Explicit wiring**: You control exactly which mocks are passed to the constructor, no hidden resolution logic
**Compile-time safety**: If constructor signature changes, your test fails to compile — immediate feedback
**No silent failures**: Unlike at-InjectMocks, if you forget a mock, you get a compile error or obvious null at construction time
**Multiple configurations**: Easy to test different constructor overloads by calling different constructors in different tests
**Conditional setup**: You can use if/else in at-BeforeEach to pass different mocks based on test conditions
**Debuggability**: Step through the constructor call in your debugger — you see exactly what's being passed
**No Mockito magic**: Your test doesn't depend on Mockito's injection resolution order or reflection behavior

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To manually inject mocks without at-InjectMocks, you just create the mocks and pass them to the constructor yourself. Here's the pattern. First, declare your mock fields with at-Mock. Then, in at-BeforeEach, construct the class under test by calling new and passing those mocks as arguments. So if you're testing OrderService, you'd do orderService equals new OrderService with mockRepository and mockPaymentService. That's it. No at-InjectMocks annotation at all. Why would you do this instead of using at-InjectMocks? A few reasons. First, it's explicit. You can see exactly what's being injected, and if you get the order wrong, the code won't compile. With at-InjectMocks, you might not discover a wiring problem until the test runs. Second, it gives you flexibility. Maybe you want to test two different constructors — one with three dependencies, one with two. You can just call different constructors in different at-BeforeEach methods or even in individual tests. Third, it's easier to debug. You can set a breakpoint on the constructor call and step into it. With at-InjectMocks, Mockito does the wiring via reflection, so you can't easily see what's happening. The trade-off is a bit more boilerplate — you have to write the new statement yourself. But in complex tests, that explicitness is worth it. If I'm testing a simple service with one constructor, I'll use at-InjectMocks. If I'm dealing with conditional logic or multiple configurations, I'll do it manually.

questions.question: What is @MockBean in Spring Boot testing and how does it differ from @Mock?
questions.title: @MockBean vs @Mock Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @MockBean replaces a bean in the Spring application context with a Mockito mock. @Mock creates a standalone Mockito mock without loading Spring. Use @Mock for unit tests (fast), @MockBean for integration tests where the Spring context must be loaded.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the boundary between unit tests and Spring integration tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using at-MockBean in unit tests — unnecessarily loads the Spring context, making tests slow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that at-MockBean invalidates the Spring context cache, causing re-load — a performance concern in large test suites

sections.title: Spring Boot @MockBean vs Mockito @Mock
sections.content: **@Mock** is a pure Mockito annotation that creates a mock object in your test without any Spring involvement. WHY use it: for fast unit tests where you test a single class in isolation. **@MockBean** is a Spring Boot annotation (from spring-boot-test) that replaces a bean in the application context with a Mockito mock. WHY use it: when you need to test a component that depends on other Spring-managed beans, but you want to mock some of those beans instead of using the real ones. HOW @MockBean works: Spring Boot starts the application context (slow operation), then swaps out the specified bean with a mock. The rest of the context is real. The critical trade-off: **@MockBean requires loading the Spring context**, which can take seconds. @Mock is instantaneous. A unit test with @Mock runs in milliseconds; an integration test with @MockBean can take 5-10 seconds. Think of @Mock as testing a single gear in isolation, @MockBean as testing the whole engine but replacing one piston with a fake one.

sections.title: @Mock (Unit Test) vs @MockBean (Integration Test)
Key Points
content: **@Mock speed**: Creates mocks instantly without Spring — ideal for unit tests targeting single classes
**@MockBean overhead**: Loads the entire Spring application context, adding 5-10 seconds per test class startup
**Context caching issue**: Each unique @MockBean configuration creates a new context, bypassing Spring's test context cache
**Integration test use case**: Use @MockBean when testing a Spring component like a controller or service that needs autowiring
**Unit test principle**: Use @Mock when you can construct the class under test manually without Spring
**@WebMvcTest optimization**: Loads only the web layer, not the full context, making @MockBean faster than @SpringBootTest
**Test pyramid guidance**: Most tests should be fast unit tests with @Mock; reserve @MockBean for a smaller number of integration tests

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The key difference is whether you need Spring's application context. At-Mock is a pure Mockito annotation. It creates a mock object in your test without starting Spring at all. You'd use this for unit tests where you're testing a single service class in isolation. You create the service manually in your test, passing the mocks to the constructor. It's fast — the test runs in milliseconds. At-MockBean is a Spring Boot annotation. It tells Spring to load the application context but replace a specific bean with a Mockito mock. You'd use this when you need to test a Spring-managed component like a controller that depends on other beans, but you want to mock one of those dependencies instead of using the real implementation. The downside is that at-MockBean requires starting the Spring context, which can take several seconds. Here's a gotcha: Spring normally caches the test context across test classes to save time. But each unique configuration of at-MockBean creates a different context, so Spring can't reuse it. If you have ten test classes all with different at-MockBean setups, you'll load the context ten times. That's why you want to minimize at-MockBean. Use at-Mock for fast unit tests whenever possible. Only reach for at-MockBean when you genuinely need the Spring wiring — like testing a REST controller with at-WebMvcTest, where the controller needs to be autowired but you want to mock the service layer. That's the trade-off: at-Mock gives you speed, at-MockBean gives you integration with Spring's dependency injection.

questions.question: What happens when @InjectMocks cannot inject a mock?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Silent Injection Failure
questions.direct_answer: Mockito silently skips the injection and leaves the field null, causing NullPointerException in tests. Using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with strict stubs helps surface these issues earlier by failing on unused mocks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you are aware of this silent failure mode that causes confusing NullPointerExceptions in tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming at-InjectMocks will throw a clear error if injection fails — it does not, it silently continues
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that strict stubbing mode helps indirectly by failing on unused stubs, and that constructor injection in production code avoids this entirely

sections.title: Silent Failure Mode of @InjectMocks
sections.content: **@InjectMocks silent failure** is one of the most frustrating behaviors in Mockito for beginners. WHY it's dangerous: when Mockito can't inject a mock (no matching constructor, no matching setter, field type mismatch), it doesn't throw an error. It just leaves the field **null**. Your test compiles and starts running, then crashes with **NullPointerException** when the code under test tries to use that dependency. HOW to detect this: the stack trace shows an NPE inside your service's business logic, not in test setup. The root cause: Mockito couldn't find a way to inject your mock. Common scenarios: the class under test has no constructor that matches your mock types, or the constructor parameter names don't align (though Mockito matches by type, not name). The fix: either add a matching constructor, use manual injection in @BeforeEach, or enable **strict stubbing** mode with MockitoExtension, which makes unused mocks fail the test. Think of @InjectMocks like an auto-installer that silently skips steps when it hits a problem, leaving you with a half-assembled machine.

sections.title: Silent Failure Example and Fix
Key Points
content: **Silent continuation**: Mockito does not throw an error when at-InjectMocks fails — it leaves fields null
**NullPointerException symptom**: Tests crash inside business logic when null dependencies are accessed, not during setup
**Strict stubbing benefit**: MockitoExtension enables strict mode, which fails on unused stubs and helps surface injection issues earlier
**Constructor mismatch cause**: If the class under test has no constructor matching your mock types, injection silently fails
**Debugging technique**: Check the test setup — if a field is null after at-InjectMocks runs, Mockito couldn't inject it
**Manual injection alternative**: Constructing the object yourself in at-BeforeEach eliminates this failure mode entirely
**Production code design**: Using constructor injection in production makes at-InjectMocks reliable and predictable

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: If at-InjectMocks can't inject a mock, Mockito just silently skips it and leaves that field null. Your test compiles fine, starts running, and then crashes with a NullPointerException the moment your code tries to use that dependency. That's incredibly confusing because the stack trace points to your business logic, not the test setup. So you're staring at your service code thinking something's wrong there, when actually the problem is that Mockito couldn't wire up your mocks. Here's why it happens. Let's say you have a mock for EmailService, but your OrderService constructor only takes an OrderRepository. Mockito tries constructor injection first, sees there's no parameter for EmailService, then tries setters and fields. If none of those match, it just gives up. It doesn't tell you. The field stays null. When your test calls a method that needs emailService, boom — NullPointerException. How do you catch this early? First, use at-ExtendWith with MockitoExtension. That enables strict stubbing mode, which fails the test if you declare a mock but never use it. That's an indirect signal that your mock isn't wired up. Second, look at your constructor. If you've got at-Mock fields that don't appear in the constructor signature, that's a red flag. Third, and honestly the best approach, is to not use at-InjectMocks at all for complex setups. Just construct the object manually in at-BeforeEach. If you forget a parameter, you get a compile error immediately. No mystery NPEs. The takeaway: at-InjectMocks is convenient for simple cases, but when it fails, it fails silently. Constructor injection in production code makes this problem go away.

questions.question: How does Mockito decide between constructor injection and field injection for @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Constructor vs Field Injection in @InjectMocks
questions.direct_answer: Mockito tries constructor injection first (using the largest constructor that matches available mocks), then setter injection, then field injection as a fallback. Constructor injection is safest because it makes dependencies explicit and fails at compile time if types don't match.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Mockito's injection resolution order and why constructor injection is the safest option
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Mockito always uses field injection; not knowing that constructor injection is attempted first and is safer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect this to Spring's own injection preference: constructor injection is favored in both production Spring code and Mockito tests for the same reason — it makes dependencies explicit

sections.title: Mockito's Injection Resolution Strategy
sections.content: **Mockito's injection order** is a three-phase algorithm that determines how @InjectMocks wires up dependencies. WHY this order matters: it affects predictability and debuggability of your tests. HOW it works: Phase 1 is **constructor injection** — Mockito scans all constructors, finds the largest one (most parameters) that can be satisfied by the available @Mock fields (matching by type), and calls it. If no constructor matches, Phase 2 is **setter injection** — Mockito looks for methods named setX where X matches a mock type (like setOrderRepository for an OrderRepository mock). If that fails, Phase 3 is **field injection** — Mockito uses reflection to directly set private fields. The key insight: **constructor injection is tried first**, making it the most reliable. If your production code uses constructor injection (which is Spring's recommendation), @InjectMocks will resolve dependencies via the constructor, avoiding the ambiguity of setter or field injection. Think of it as a preference list: Mockito asks for the front door key first (constructor), then the side door (setter), then breaks a window if necessary (field reflection).

sections.title: Constructor Injection Preference in Action
Key Points
content: **Constructor first**: Mockito always tries constructor injection before setter or field injection
**Largest constructor preference**: Mockito picks the constructor with the most parameters that can be satisfied by available mocks
**Type matching**: Mockito matches constructor parameters to mocks by type, not by variable name
**Setter fallback**: If no constructor works, Mockito looks for setX methods matching mock types (uncommon in modern code)
**Field injection last resort**: Reflection-based field injection is the final fallback if constructor and setter fail
**Spring alignment**: Both Spring and Mockito prefer constructor injection — using it in production makes tests predictable
**Silent failure risk**: If none of the three strategies work, Mockito creates the object with null fields without error

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mockito decides between constructor and field injection by trying them in a specific order. Constructor injection is always attempted first. Here's how it works. Mockito looks at all the constructors in your class under test. It picks the largest constructor — the one with the most parameters — that it can satisfy with the mocks you've declared. If you have three at-Mock fields and a constructor that takes all three as parameters, Mockito will call that constructor, passing your mocks as arguments. If there's no constructor that matches, Mockito moves to phase two: setter injection. It looks for methods like setOrderRepository or setPaymentService that match your mock types. That's pretty rare in modern Spring code, though. If setter injection also fails, Mockito falls back to field injection. It uses reflection to directly set your private fields, even if they're not accessible. That works, but it's the least predictable option. Here's why constructor injection being first is so important. If you follow Spring's recommendation and use constructor injection in your production code, at-InjectMocks will reliably use that constructor. You get predictable behavior. But if your production code uses field injection, Mockito has to use reflection, and you lose some type safety. The other thing to know is that this is the same preference order as Spring itself. Spring also tries constructor injection first, then setter, then field. So by aligning your production code with this pattern — using constructor injection — you make both Spring and Mockito happy. Your tests become more predictable, and you avoid the silent failure mode where Mockito can't wire things up.

sections.title: Testing Constructor Injection Without @InjectMocks
sections.content: **Manual construction** is the simplest way to test a class that uses constructor injection. WHY do this: you avoid @InjectMocks's silent failure mode and gain complete control over how dependencies are wired. HOW it works: declare your mocks with @Mock (or create them with Mockito.mock()), then in @BeforeEach, instantiate the class under test by calling new and passing the mocks as constructor arguments. The benefit: if you forget a parameter or pass the wrong type, you get a **compile-time error**, not a runtime NullPointerException. When to prefer this over @InjectMocks: always, unless you're testing a class with a very large number of dependencies where manually listing them all is tedious. For most service classes with 2-4 dependencies, manual construction is clearer and more debuggable. The key insight: **@InjectMocks is optional automation**. It's not a requirement for testing. Think of @InjectMocks as autocomplete for constructor arguments — convenient when it works, but you can always type the arguments yourself for full control.

sections.title: Explicit Constructor Injection in Tests
Key Points
content: **Explicit wiring**: You call the constructor yourself with mock arguments — no hidden resolution logic
**Compile-time safety**: If the constructor signature changes, your test won't compile until you fix it
**No silent failures**: Missing a mock parameter results in a compilation error, not a runtime NullPointerException
**Debuggability**: Step through the constructor call in the debugger to see exactly what's being passed
**Flexibility**: Easily test different constructor overloads by calling different constructors in different tests
**No Mockito magic**: The test doesn't depend on Mockito's injection resolution order or reflection behavior
**Best practice alignment**: Mirrors production code — if you use constructor injection in services, tests naturally follow the same pattern

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: If your class uses constructor injection, you don't need at-InjectMocks at all. Just pass the mocks to the constructor yourself. Here's the pattern. First, declare your mock dependencies with at-Mock. Then, in at-BeforeEach, create the object under test by calling new and passing those mocks as arguments. So if you're testing OrderService, you'd write orderService equals new OrderService with mockRepository, mockPaymentService, and mockNotificationService. That's it. No annotations on the orderService field, no at-InjectMocks. Why is this better than at-InjectMocks? Three big reasons. First, it's explicit. You can see exactly what's being passed and in what order. If you mess up — maybe you pass mockPaymentService twice by accident — the compiler catches it because the types don't match. With at-InjectMocks, Mockito figures it out at runtime, and if something goes wrong, you get a cryptic NPE. Second, if the constructor signature changes — say someone adds a new dependency — your test won't compile until you add that parameter. That's immediate feedback. With at-InjectMocks, the test might still compile but fail at runtime. Third, it's trivial to debug. You can set a breakpoint on the new statement and step into the constructor to see what's happening. With at-InjectMocks, Mockito does the wiring via reflection, so it's harder to trace. The only downside to manual construction is if you have a service with ten dependencies. Then writing out all ten arguments is tedious. But honestly, if a class has ten dependencies, that's a code smell — it probably violates the Single Responsibility Principle. For normal services with two to four dependencies, manual construction is the way to go. It's clearer, safer, and easier to maintain.

questions.question: What is @MockBean and how does it differ from @Mock when testing Spring Boot applications?
questions.title: @MockBean vs @Mock in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @Mock is a pure Mockito annotation for unit tests with no Spring context; @MockBean is a Spring Boot annotation that adds a Mockito mock to the Spring application context, replacing the real bean. Use @Mock for fast unit tests, @MockBean for integration tests where Spring wiring is needed.

sections.title: Context Boundaries: @Mock vs @MockBean
sections.content: **@Mock** is a Mockito annotation that creates a standalone mock without Spring. WHY use it: for **unit tests** where you test a single class in isolation, constructing it manually. **@MockBean** is a Spring Boot test annotation that replaces a bean in the Spring application context with a mock. WHY use it: for **integration tests** where you need Spring to wire up your components, but you want to replace one or more beans with mocks instead of the real implementation. HOW @MockBean works: Spring Boot loads the full application context (or a slice of it with @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest), then swaps out the specified bean with a mock. The rest of the context is real. The trade-off: **@MockBean is slow** because it requires starting Spring. A unit test with @Mock runs in milliseconds; an integration test with @MockBean can take 5-10 seconds per test class. Worse, each unique @MockBean configuration creates a new context, bypassing Spring's context cache. Think of @Mock as testing a gear in isolation on your workbench; @MockBean as testing the gear inside the engine, but you've replaced one piston with a dummy.

sections.title: Unit Test (@Mock) vs Integration Test (@MockBean)
Key Points
content: **@Mock speed**: Instantaneous mock creation, no Spring startup — ideal for unit tests
**@MockBean overhead**: Requires loading Spring context, adding 5-10 seconds per test class
**Context caching problem**: Each unique @MockBean configuration creates a new context, bypassing Spring's cache
**Integration test boundary**: Use @MockBean when you need @Autowired dependencies or are testing a Spring slice like @WebMvcTest
**Unit test isolation**: Use @Mock when you can construct the class under test without Spring
**Slice annotations optimization**: @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest load only part of the context, making @MockBean faster than @SpringBootTest
**Test pyramid guidance**: Most tests should be fast unit tests with @Mock; reserve @MockBean for critical integration paths

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-Mock and at-MockBean solve different problems. At-Mock is pure Mockito. It creates a mock object in your test without starting Spring at all. You'd use this for unit tests where you're testing a single service in isolation. You create the service manually in your test, passing the mocks to the constructor. It's incredibly fast — the test runs in milliseconds because there's no framework overhead. At-MockBean is a Spring Boot annotation. It tells Spring to load the application context, but replace a specific bean with a Mockito mock. You'd use this when you're writing an integration test — like testing a REST controller with at-WebMvcTest — where you need Spring to wire up the controller, but you want to mock the service layer so you're not hitting a real database. The problem with at-MockBean is it's slow. Starting the Spring context takes several seconds. Here's a bigger gotcha: Spring normally caches the test context across test classes to save time. But each unique configuration of at-MockBean creates a different context, so Spring can't reuse it. If you have five test classes all mocking different beans, you'll start Spring five times. That's why you want to minimize at-MockBean usage. Use at-Mock whenever you can test in isolation. Only reach for at-MockBean when you genuinely need Spring's wiring — like when testing a controller that needs to be autowired, or when you're using a Spring slice annotation like at-DataJpaTest to load just the persistence layer. That's the key decision point: do I need the Spring context for this test? If no, use at-Mock. If yes, use at-MockBean, but be aware of the performance cost.
